source: Piantadosi, Tenenbaum & Goodman (2012) Bootstrapping in a language of thought
finding: Core LoT model: a hypothesis is a short program (lambda-calculus expression) built from a small set of primitives. The learner does Bayesian inference over all compositions, so concepts are programs scored by prior (shorter = likelier) times fit to data.
numbers: Primitives include singleton?, doubleton?, tripleton?, set ops (union, intersection, difference, select), logic (and, or, not, if), next/prev on the count list, and the recursive call L. Hypothesis space is infinite. Search by MCMC over 1 to 1000 data points.
limits: It is an existence proof, not proof that children do this. Primitives were chosen by the authors.
agent_relevance: S2 REPRESENT as 'write the rule as a short program from a small named primitive set' and S3 GENERATE as sampling compositions, with a length prior built in.

source: Piantadosi, Tenenbaum & Goodman (2012) Bootstrapping in a language of thought: prior
finding: The prior is the rational-rules prior: it favours reuse of primitives and penalises long expressions. A separate extra penalty (parameter c) is placed on recursive lexicons.
numbers: Free parameters: noise a (reported run a=0.75) and recursion cost log c=-25. With no recursion penalty the model makes the jump to the recursive rule roughly after becoming a 1-knower (too early). With log c=-100 it stays a 4-knower for a long time.
limits: The timing of the key transition depends on a free parameter, so the model does not strongly predict when it happens. The authors say this themselves.
agent_relevance: Shows the one knob that sets how fast a scaffold should prefer a general (recursive or abstract) rule over a list of special cases: the complexity price of generality.

source: Piantadosi, Tenenbaum & Goodman (2012) Bootstrapping in a language of thought: likelihood and undef
finding: The likelihood prefers staying silent (undef) over a wrong guess. A rule that says 'one' for singletons and nothing else beats a rule that says 'one' for every set. This produces stages where later words are left unassigned, as in children.
numbers: A word under a hypothesis that returns undef has likelihood 1/N; an incorrect prediction has likelihood (1-a)/N. Training pairs were drawn from CHILDES transcripts of children aged 20 to 40 months, with word frequency falling off like a power law.
quote: Bayes' theorem implements a simple trade-off between complexity and fit to data
limits: Word frequencies came from raw counts of all number-word tokens, including non-numerical uses such as 'give me one'.
agent_relevance: A partial rule that abstains on uncovered cases beats an over-general wrong rule when data are thin. Whether a rule covers a case is cheap for code to check.

source: Piantadosi, Tenenbaum & Goodman (2012) Bootstrapping in a language of thought: developmental curve
finding: The model passes through 1-knower, 2-knower, 3-knower, (4-knower) and then a sudden shift to a recursive CP-knower rule, the same order seen in children. The shift happens because more data than the subset rules can explain finally pays for the longer recursive program.
numbers: Learning curves are marginal posterior mass per behaviour type over 1 to 1000 data points. Children's published pattern: about a year at the first 3-4 words, then a sudden shift near age 3;6.
limits: Fit to the qualitative order and the sudden shift, not to a fitted quantitative curve. Time axis is amount of data, not age.
agent_relevance: A sudden jump to a better representation is predicted by a complexity-versus-fit trade-off, not by a special 'insight' module. This weakens the case for adding a separate insight operator.

source: Piantadosi, Tenenbaum & Goodman (2012) Bootstrapping in a language of thought: Mod-5 control
finding: Natural number is not hard-wired. When the data were relabelled with a Mod-5 system the same model learned Mod-5, going through the same subset stages first. With singular/plural data it learned singular/plural quickly.
numbers: Mod-5 data are identical to natural-number data for set sizes 1 to 5, then sizes 6, 7 are paired with 'one', 'two'. A Mod-N primitive was deliberately left out of the language; special MCMC proposals were needed for the Mod-5 case.
limits: Mod-N is much more complex than the CP rule, so with real child data it gets low probability. The model would predict very different timing if Mod were a primitive.
agent_relevance: Evidence that the representation language fixes what is learnable, but the data pick among rules inside it. The set of primitives is where the prior knowledge lives.

source: Piantadosi, Tenenbaum & Goodman (2012) Bootstrapping in a language of thought: critiques
finding: The authors state the critique that bootstrapping presupposes a number-isomorphic system (Rips et al.), and note their version differs from Carey's: the jump is driven by data volume, not by analogy.
numbers: Prediction stated by the authors: a child shown only the first three number words would never make the jump, because a 3-knower rule explains the data better.
limits: Untested prediction. Later critics (Asmuth; Rey) argue the model recombines existing primitives and does not create genuinely new ones; those papers were not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Warns that 'new concept' in an LoT model may just be a new composition. For an agent, the library of primitives bounds what it can express at S2.

source: Goodman, Tenenbaum, Feldman & Griffiths (2008) A rational analysis of rule-based concept learning (CogSci 2007 conference version read)
finding: Rational Rules model: concepts are formulas in disjunctive normal form generated by a grammar, with a prior favouring short formulas, a likelihood with an outlier parameter b, and posterior by Bayes. One free parameter.
numbers: Fit to Medin & Schaffer (1978) category structure (human data from the Nosofsky et al. 1994 replication): R2=0.98 for Rational Rules, 0.98 for RULEX (nine free parameters), 0.96 for the context model.
limits: DNF form is assumed in advance. Fits are on group-average generalization. This is the conference version, not the 2008 journal paper.
agent_relevance: Gives a clean template: prior by length, likelihood tolerant of noise, posterior over rules. The outlier term is a built-in guard against fitting noisy examples exactly.

source: Goodman et al. (2008) rational rules: individual differences
finding: If each person holds one formula sampled from the posterior, the model explains individual generalization patterns, and it predicts the prototype effect without a prototype mechanism.
numbers: 36 individual generalization patterns from Nosofsky et al. (1994) Experiment 1: R2=0.83 with the one-sample-per-person assumption. Prototype T3=0000 is the most likely transfer item classed as category A, as in humans.
limits: The authors call deterministic single-rule use troubling given graded typicality effects inside individuals. Preference for simple rules along features 1 and 3 reproduces selective attention.
agent_relevance: Sampling one program per run and aggregating across runs reproduces the human group pattern. This matches sample-then-vote designs, with the caution of G4 that samples from one model are correlated.

source: Piantadosi, Tenenbaum & Goodman (2016) The logical primitives of thought: experiment
finding: Large web experiment on learning rule-based concepts: participants learned an alien word 'wudsy' from labelled sets of shapes, 25 sets, labelling each object. Concepts included Boolean and quantified (relational) rules.
numbers: 108 concepts, 1,596 participants (Mechanical Turk), about 20 per concept and list, two lists per concept. Overall accuracy 78% against chance 56%. Mean concept accuracy correlated across the two lists at R2=0.81. 3.9% of data removed on average.
limits: Online sample. Written descriptions at sets 5, 10, 25 were too ambiguous to analyse; the authors take this as mild evidence that people do not hold the concept as an English sentence.
agent_relevance: Rule learning from few labelled examples is a standard human skill that scaffolds can mimic by proposing and testing rules. The ambiguity of written descriptions is a warning about verbal rule statements at S2.

source: Piantadosi, Tenenbaum & Goodman (2016) The logical primitives of thought: model comparison
finding: A memory-limited Bayesian program-learning model with an inferred grammar explains held-out human responses far better than exemplar or feature-only models. Models with no simplicity bias do worse.
numbers: On held-out data the best grammar (FULLBOOLEAN) explains 88% of variation in participants' response patterns. The EXEMPLAR model explains only about half. FULLBOOLEAN beat IMPLIES, HORNCLAUSE, NAND and NOR significantly (Wilcoxon, Bonferroni, p<.05) but not BICONDITIONAL, CNF, DNF or SIMPLEBOOLEAN. One run took about 50 processor days.
limits: Resolution cannot separate the top four grammars. Held-out likelihood gap to the closest competitor was about 8 points.
agent_relevance: Strong quantitative support that simplicity-weighted program search predicts human generalization, and that unstructured similarity does not.

source: Piantadosi, Tenenbaum & Goodman (2016) The logical primitives of thought: which primitives
finding: People appear to have a richer set of logical connectives than just and, or, not. Adding iff (biconditional) helped; Horn-clause form, common in AI, fit worse. Single-primitive NAND or NOR languages fit worse.
numbers: Grammars with iff and the normal forms (DNF, CNF) did best; SIMPLEBOOLEAN (free-form and/or/not) was worse than FULLBOOLEAN. XOR-type concepts such as 'red XOR circle' account for most of the iff advantage.
limits: Differences among the top grammars were within noise (see previous line). The paper itself says primitives are inferred only up to this resolution.
agent_relevance: Which primitives to give the agent is an empirical question. Minimal primitive sets are not what people use; a redundant, richer set matches human difficulty better.

source: Piantadosi, Tenenbaum & Goodman (2016) The logical primitives of thought: simplicity logic
finding: The paper's design logic: if people find 'red OR square' easier than 'red XOR square' then XOR is not primitive. Difficulty tracks description length in the mental language (follows Feldman 2000).
numbers: Cites Feldman (2000, 2003) for Boolean description length predicting difficulty. Feldman's primary papers were not opened by this agent.
limits: Secondhand for Feldman. Grue-style objection: simplicity is language-relative; Kolmogorov complexity fixes it only up to a constant.
agent_relevance: Length of the shortest program in a given language is a usable difficulty proxy; a scaffold can use program length as a prior and as a signal to doubt (G1).

source: Lake, Salakhutdinov & Tenenbaum (2015) Human-level concept learning through probabilistic program induction (BPL)
finding: Bayesian Program Learning: a character concept is a generative program of strokes (parts, sub-parts, relations). One example is parsed into a program, then used to classify and to generate new examples. Three principles: compositionality, causality, learning to learn.
numbers: One-shot classification of new characters among 20 (chance 95% error): people 4.5% error (N=40), BPL 3.3%, deep convnet 13.5%, deep Siamese convnet 8.0%, Hausdorff baseline 38.8%. Lesions: no learning-to-learn 11.0%, no compositionality 14.0%.
limits: Hand-built stroke grammar for one domain (handwritten characters). Whether the approach scales to open domains is not shown.
agent_relevance: Program representation beat much larger neural models in the low-data regime on a concept task. The ablations show each principle contributes: a model for ablation tests in our own schema.

source: Lake et al. (2015) BPL: visual Turing tests
finding: Generating new examples is also good: judges could barely tell BPL drawings from human drawings. Lesioned models were easy to spot.
numbers: Judges (N=147) identified the machine at 52% average (ideal 50%); t(47)=2.03, P=0.048; only 3 of 48 judges reliably above chance. Lesion without learning-to-learn: 80% identification; without compositionality: 65%. Dynamic version (N=143): 59%.
limits: Identification rates near 50% show indistinguishability on this task only.
agent_relevance: Generation from a program, not from a surface pattern, gave human-like variation. Supports generating by program (S3) when diversity and validity both matter.

source: Johnson, Vong, Lake & Gureckis (2021) Fast and flexible: human program induction in abstract reasoning tasks
finding: First behavioural study of people on ARC. People infer the hidden program and apply it to a new input quickly; difficulty rises with description length.
numbers: 40 ARC tasks, 95 Mechanical Turk participants, three attempts per task. Mean 83.8% correct per task (SD 16.7%); 80% of tasks solved per participant; 65% of tasks solved by 80% or more of participants. Hardest task 38.1%. The Kaggle program-synthesis winner got 57.5% on the same 40 tasks (21% on the hidden test set); Spearman correlation with humans 0.35, p<.05. Logistic mixed model: longer average description length, b=-0.17, 95% CI [-0.315,-0.020], p=0.03.
limits: Only 40 of 1000 tasks, all from the training set. The synthesizer lacked human-like object-centred intermediate states.
agent_relevance: Humans solve ARC with short object-level rules; description length predicts failure. Our own runs where programs fit all examples yet were wrong (G3) fit this.

source: Acquaviva, Pu, Kryven et al. (2022) Communicating natural programs to humans and machines (LARC)
finding: Two-player game: one person describes an ARC task in words, another must build the output. 88% of ARC tasks could be communicated by language alone. Natural programs mix procedures with framing and examples.
numbers: 88% of ARC tasks language-complete. Program synthesizers conditioned on the natural-language descriptions solved at best 22 of 183 test tasks (best 12%); with language only, no more than 1 task. Input-output checking was crucial for the synthesizer.
quote: the overall results (best 12%) are still comically bad.
limits: Synthesizers were enumerative with a bigram prior, 2021-era, not LLMs.
agent_relevance: Humans share rules as short natural programs; execution against examples is what made them work. Checking with examples (code) matters more than the wording of the rule.

source: Ellis et al. (2021) DreamCoder: growing generalizable, interpretable knowledge with wake-sleep Bayesian program learning
finding: Wake-sleep program induction: wake = search for programs that solve tasks using a neural recogniser; abstraction sleep = compress solutions into new library functions; dreaming sleep = train the recogniser on programs sampled from the library. The library grows in layers.
numbers: List processing: 218 problems split 50/50, about 20 new routines learned; it rediscovered filter, then max, nth largest, then sort. Text editing: 128 training tasks, test on 108 SyGuS 2017 problems: 3.7% before learning, 79.6% after, mean solve time 235s to 40s. CVC4 82.4% (1 hour, 8 CPUs); DreamCoder 84.3% with that budget.
limits: Needs 100 or more training tasks per domain. A hand-set starting primitive set for each domain. Enumerative search is slow.
agent_relevance: The library-learning idea behind a memory of solved subgoals. Numbers show gains come from reusable abstractions plus guided search together.

source: Ellis et al. (2021) DreamCoder: ablations and domains
finding: Ablations without the recogniser (dreaming) or without abstraction solve fewer tasks. Memorising whole solutions as primitives, without compression, does worse. Eight domains in all, including LOGO graphics (160 images), towers (107), regex (256 CSV columns), symbolic regression, and 60 physics laws.
numbers: Five runs per condition, 20 wake-sleep cycles; baselines included Enumeration (24 hours per task, up to 400 million programs), RobustFill neural synthesis, Exploration-Compression, and two Memorize variants. Exact per-domain percentages are only in Fig. 6 and were not tabulated in the text.
limits: Reported mainly as plots; this line gives the design, not a table.
agent_relevance: Compression into shared abstractions, not storing every solved case, is what generalises; relevant to how an agent should store solved subproblems.

source: Ellis (2023) Human-like few-shot learning via Bayesian reasoning over natural language (NeurIPS)
finding: Concepts are expressed in natural language. An LLM proposes candidate concept sentences from the examples, a learned prior reweights them, and Bayes picks. The LLM is the proposal distribution, not the judge.
numbers: Number Game: fits an average of 8 human raters with 50 to 100 samples; the original model used over 5000 hypotheses. Logical concept task (data of Piantadosi et al. 2016): R2=0.81 with 100 proposals per batch, within 3% of human accuracy; GPT-4 alone fits worse. 16 new participants on 2 new concepts. A tuned prior was critical for the logic task.
limits: Abstract symbolic concepts only, not perceptual ones. The number-game human data are from only 8 raters. The pretrained prior alone is sensitive to syntax.
agent_relevance: Direct blueprint for S3: LLM proposes rules in words, code scores them against the data; selection is by prior plus fit, not LLM opinion (matches G5, G8).

source: Wang, Zelikman, Poesia, Pu, Haber & Goodman (2024) Hypothesis search: inductive reasoning with language models (ICLR)
finding: GPT-4 proposes abstract hypotheses in words, then writes Python for each, and the programs are run on the examples. Filtering hypotheses by LLM summary or by human choice helps.
numbers: 100 random ARC tasks (GPT-4): direct prompting 17%; programs without hypotheses 23%; with summarized hypotheses 30%; human-selected from 64 LLM hypotheses 33%; human-written LARC hypotheses 33%. Icecuber DSL search 43%. Chain-of-thought with intermediate language but no program: 19%. A human found a correct hypothesis for 49 tasks; 33 (67%) gave correct programs.
limits: They report a low false-positive rate on these datasets but say a program that passes the training examples can still be wrong. Numbers are for GPT-4 (March 2023).
agent_relevance: Program representation lifts accuracy (17 to 23) and abstract hypotheses add more (23 to 30). Language reasoning with no executable program did not help (19).

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis search: other benchmarks
finding: On SyGuS string tasks GPT-4 direct program writing already solves almost all; the hypothesis step adds nothing there. On List Functions the hypotheses help.
numbers: SyGuS: 94.3% with 8 programs and two rounds of feedback, with or without hypotheses (CrossBeam 74.8% with a DSL of 50K candidates); 3 of the 5 failures were errors in the examples. List Functions: 47.5% with human-written hypotheses vs 37.5% directly generating programs, on 40 questions. ARC with 128 GPT-3.5 programs: 27%.
limits: Small sample (40 questions) in the List Functions comparison.
agent_relevance: An abstract-hypothesis step only pays on tasks where the first program guess is far from the answer. A scaffold should test per task family whether it helps.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal yet puzzling: testing inductive reasoning with hypothesis refinement (ICLR)
finding: Iterated propose, select, refine of text rules with a symbolic interpreter filter. LMs are strong proposers but poor at applying their own rules, and brittle to noisy examples.
numbers: ACRE raw accuracy: IO prompting 64.0 vs refinement (T=3, N=5) 82.5; ACRE task accuracy 28.0 vs 59.0. MiniARC raw accuracy: IO 33.1 vs 18.7 (refinement worse). MiniSCAN task accuracy drops from over 80% with a symbolic interpreter to almost zero when the LM itself applies its rule. Self-consistency majority vote did not help as much as hypothesis selection.
limits: Text-only models on MiniARC; a multimodal model did worse. One perturbed example in 8 already hurts, and a warning in the prompt only partly fixes it.
agent_relevance: Execution of a rule must be by code, not by the model (G1/G2/G5). Majority voting alone is not a substitute for rule selection by an interpreter.

source: Qiu et al. (2024): human comparison and noise
finding: Cited human data: 3-4 year-old children find a 'blicket' within 2 trials (ACRE; Gopnik 2001, Sobel 2004). Noise test: 12.5%, 25%, 50% of 8 exemplars perturbed; LM accuracy falls steadily.
numbers: The gap between raw and task accuracy shows many correct outputs come without following the intended rule (IO and self-consistency especially).
limits: Human noise data were gathered on Mechanical Turk in a separate small study described in the appendix.
agent_relevance: Raw accuracy can overstate rule learning. Evaluate whether one rule explains every example, not only the final answer.

source: Li, Hu, Larsen et al. (2024) Combining induction and transduction for abstract reasoning
finding: Two neural models trained on the same synthetic ARC data: one writes a Python program (induction), one outputs the grid (transduction). They solve different problems, stably across seeds. Induction is better at precise computation and composing concepts; transduction at fuzzy perceptual ones.
numbers: Ensemble 56.75% on ARC validation (average human 60.2%, best human 97.8%); with better test-time training Akyurek et al. reached 61.9% using the induction model as is. Induction at 2048 samples vs transduction beam 20: 18.78% vs 15.25% in one fine-tuning setting, 11.07% vs 13.50% in another; ensembles 26.50% and 19.50%.
quote: Inductive program synthesis excels at precise computations, and at composing multiple concepts
limits: The 56.75% figure uses test-time training and reranking. Val Acc counts 2 tries. About 9% of samples that fit the training examples are false positives.
agent_relevance: About 9% of program samples that fit the training examples are wrong: G3 evidence. About half of that 9% would be fixed by a majority vote over outputs. Programs and direct answers are complementary, so offer both and select by code.

source: Li et al. (2024): scaling and human difficulty
finding: Induction solve rate rises almost monotonically with number of samples. On five difficulty tiers, all models beat people on the hardest 20% of problems and trail them on the easiest 20%.
numbers: False-positive rate about 9% of passing samples; roughly half of those have a majority-vote answer that is still the correct one.
limits: Human difficulty data come from LeGris et al. (2024), not collected in this paper.
agent_relevance: Where a short program exists, search scales with samples; where humans use priors that the program language lacks, search fails. Program-language coverage is the limit.

source: Wong, Grand, Lew, Goodman, Mansinghka, Andreas & Tenenbaum (2023) From word models to world models
finding: Proposes rational meaning construction: an LLM translates each sentence into code (Church conditions and queries), and a probabilistic program engine does the inference. Thought is the program; language is the way into it.
numbers: Illustrated on four domains (probabilistic reasoning with the tug-of-war model, relational reasoning with kinship, visual and physical reasoning, social planning), with Codex for translation and 1000 simulated scenarios in one example. No benchmark numbers or human correlations are reported in this paper.
limits: Demonstration with worked examples, not a measured test. Translation errors are discussed only qualitatively.
agent_relevance: Pattern for S2: restate the problem as a small formal model that code can run, with an LLM only translating. Fits 'the program decides, the model fills a slot' (schema section 1).

source: Grand, Wong, Bowers, Olausson, Liu, Tenenbaum & Andreas (2024) LILO: learning interpretable libraries by compressing and documenting code (ICLR)
finding: LLM-guided synthesis, Stitch compression into abstractions, and auto-documentation of each abstraction. Compared with DreamCoder on string editing (REGEX), scene reasoning (CLEVR) and graphics (LOGO).
numbers: LILO beats DreamCoder by +33.14 points (REGEX) and +20.42 (LOGO), +2.26 on CLEVR (DreamCoder 94.50%). Plain LLM solver vs DreamCoder: +32.20 REGEX, -5.83 CLEVR, +3.60 LOGO. Adding compressed abstractions without names changed solve rate by -30.60 (REGEX), -2.91 (CLEVR), -11.11 (LOGO) vs the LLM solver; auto-documentation recovered +9.73 (REGEX) and +2.27 (CLEVR), 0.00 on LOGO. One LLM synthesis round costs about as much as 48 CPU-hours of DreamCoder search.
limits: Library names and docstrings matter: anonymous abstractions hurt. Gains depend on language annotations being available.
agent_relevance: Library entries must be named and described to be usable by an LLM. An unnamed shared function can make the model worse.

source: Berlot-Attwell, Rudzicz & Si (2024) Library learning doesn't: the curious case of the single-use library
finding: Re-analysis of two LLM library-learning systems (LEGO-Prover, TroVE). Learned functions are almost never reused; ablating cross-problem sharing leaves performance similar. Gains seem to come from self-correction and self-consistency.
numbers: Only 1,233 lemmas (6%) were used at the final proving step, and exactly one was reused once. TroVE final library had 15 learned functions; 3 successful reuses in 3,201 MATH test questions; the no-reuse ablation exceeded the baseline on three of four MATH splits. Original LEGO-Prover beat the ablation by one problem in each of two runs.
quote: function reuse is extremely infrequent on miniF2F [Zheng et al., 2022] and MATH
limits: Two systems, two datasets, a subset of questions for the LEGO-Prover ablation; the authors say they could not settle whether LLMs can reuse tools at all.
agent_relevance: Failed replication of the library-learning story for LLM agents: do not credit a library for gains that sampling and self-correction may explain. Test with a no-reuse arm at equal tokens (G7).

source: Rule, Tenenbaum & Piantadosi (2020) The child as hacker
finding: Extends the LoT view from find the shortest program to hacking: children revise code for many values (speed, clarity, reuse, memory) using many operations (add functions, debug, refactor, memoise), not only by sampling programs from a posterior.
numbers: The simplicity-plus-fit view is described as the dominant LoT proposal: balance by Bayes or minimum description length, with learners stochastically sampling candidate programs. Worked example: sum to min strategy for early addition; children keep several strategies at once.
limits: Opinion article: no new measurements. It says its predictions differ from alternatives but the tests are still to be done.
agent_relevance: Gives a catalogue of program-revision moves that an agent could trial as operators: debug, refactor, memoise. Each would have to pay at equal tokens (G7).

source: Fodor (1975) The language of thought; Boole (1854)
finding: Founding claim cited by all of the above: thought is carried by a compositional symbolic code with primitive elements and combination rules. Modern LoT work turns this into program induction with a prior over programs.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened. Cited only as given in the papers read this session.
agent_relevance: Gives the vocabulary (primitives, composition) used in the schema's S2.

source: Carey (2009) The origin of concepts; Wynn (1990, 1992); Lee & Sarnecka (2010)
finding: As described in Piantadosi et al. (2012): children are subset-knowers for about a year (know one, then two, three) and then abruptly learn the meaning of all counting words around age 3;6. Carey's bootstrapping explains this by analogy between early set-size words and the count list.
numbers: Described secondhand: roughly a year at the first 3-4 words, shift at about age 3;6. No sample sizes seen by this agent.
limits: Not opened; all figures are from the 2012 paper's own summary.
agent_relevance: Founding behavioural data the program-induction account tries to explain.

source: Shepard, Hovland & Jenkins (1961); Bruner, Goodnow & Austin (1956); Feldman (2000)
finding: Classic rule-learning experiments on logically defined categories. Difficulty of learning a Boolean concept tracks the length of its shortest logical description (Feldman 2000).
numbers: Not read; the 2016 and 2008 papers cite them as the tradition they build on.
limits: Not opened. Whether pure description-length accounts fail on some Shepard types was not checked.
agent_relevance: Basis for using description length as a prior on rule hypotheses.
